introduction_markdown: Time allowed: two and a half hours. Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1 1/2 hours; you are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER a, b and c OR d, e and f of each question. For your guidance the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation of your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the earth, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define interference. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Name the two types of interference. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Explain what happens to the resultant amplitude of each type named in (ii) above. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Interference** is the **superposition** of two (or more) waves meeting at the same point, giving a resultant displacement equal to the sum of the individual displacements.

(ii) **Constructive interference** and **destructive interference**.

(iii) In **constructive** interference the waves arrive **in phase** (crest on crest): the resultant amplitude is the **sum** of the two amplitudes, so it is **larger** than each of them. In **destructive** interference the waves arrive **out of phase** (crest on trough): the resultant amplitude is the **difference** of the two amplitudes, and it is **zero** if the two amplitudes are equal.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 3 shows how a stationary wave is formed on a string tied at both ends A and B.

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_5_fig_1.png)

*Figure 3*

(i) Calculate the wavelength of the stationary wave. *[2 marks]*

(ii) State and explain what happens to the small object placed at X. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The string AB carries **3 loops**. Each loop is half a wavelength, so

$3 \times \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 90\,\mathrm{cm}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{2 \times 90}{3} = 60\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.60\,\mathrm{m}$

**The wavelength is $60\,\mathrm{cm}$.**

(ii) X is a **node**: it is the point where the two extreme positions of the string cross. **The small object stays at rest** (it does not move or vibrate). At a node the two waves travelling in opposite directions along the string always arrive **in antiphase** and cancel each other (**destructive interference**), so the displacement there is always zero. (At an antinode, by contrast, an object would vibrate with the maximum amplitude.)
